questions.text: What is the name of the title of a magazine or newspaper, printed in large type at the top of the front cover? Give the term.

feedback.cover line: Cover lines tell readers about stories inside; the title of the publication has another name
feedback.headline: A headline is the title of a story, not of the whole publication

questions.solution: The masthead is the title of the publication, usually in a large, recognisable font at the top of the cover
questions.hint: It shares its name with the top part of a ship

questions.text: In semiotics, what is denotation?

options: The associated or emotional meanings of a sign
The literal, obvious meaning of a sign
The target audience of a text
The order in which a story is told
feedback: That is connotation

questions.solution: Denotation is the literal meaning of a sign, for example a red rose denotes a flower
questions.hint: It is the 'dictionary' meaning

questions.text: Which theorist suggested that many stories move from equilibrium, through disruption, to a new equilibrium?

options: Tzvetan Todorov
Vladimir Propp
Claude Lévi-Strauss
Stuart Hall
feedback: Propp identified character types in folk tales
Lévi-Strauss is known for binary oppositions
Stuart Hall is known for representation and reception theory

questions.solution: Tzvetan Todorov's narrative theory moves from equilibrium through disruption to a new equilibrium
questions.hint: He was a Bulgarian-French theorist of narrative

questions.text: Which theorist identified character types such as the hero, the villain, the donor and the princess by studying Russian folk tales? Give the surname.

feedback.Todorov: Todorov's theory is about equilibrium and disruption, not character types

questions.solution: Vladimir Propp analysed Russian folk tales and identified recurring character types and functions
questions.hint: He was a Russian scholar who published his study in 1928

questions.text: What does the term 'semiotics' mean?

options: The study of how media companies are owned
The measurement of audience size
The study of camera movement only
The study of signs and how they create meaning

questions.solution: Semiotics is the study of signs (words, images, colours, sounds) and how they make meaning
questions.hint: Think about signs and symbols

questions.text: Which theorist is most closely associated with the idea of binary oppositions in narratives?

options: Tzvetan Todorov
Vladimir Propp
Laura Mulvey
Claude Lévi-Strauss

questions.solution: Claude Lévi-Strauss argued that narratives are built around pairs of opposites, such as good and evil
questions.hint: He was a French anthropologist who studied myths

questions.text: What is the term for the associated, emotional or cultural meanings a sign suggests beyond its literal meaning? Give the term.

feedback.denotation: Denotation is the literal meaning; the suggested meanings are something else

questions.solution: Connotation is the set of associated meanings, for example a red rose connotes love
questions.hint: It is the opposite of denotation

questions.text: What is the difference between denotation and connotation?

options: Denotation is the associated meaning; connotation is the literal meaning
Denotation is the literal meaning; connotation is the associated meaning
Denotation is about sound; connotation is about images
Denotation is used in print; connotation is used only in film
feedback: You have swapped them round

questions.solution: Denotation is what a sign literally shows; connotation is what it suggests
questions.hint: One is literal, the other is suggested

questions.text: In Propp's character types, what does the donor do?

options: Sends the hero off on the quest
Tries to stop the hero from succeeding
Gives the hero something, such as a magic object or advice, that is needed later
Pretends to be the hero to take the reward
feedback: That is the dispatcher
That is the villain
That is the false hero

questions.solution: Propp's donor prepares the hero or gives them a magical object or advice
questions.hint: Think about what 'donate' means

questions.text: In Todorov's narrative theory, what is the name for the calm, balanced situation at the start of a story? Give the term.

feedback.disruption: The disruption is the event that upsets the calm situation
feedback.new equilibrium: The new equilibrium comes at the end of the story

questions.solution: A story begins in equilibrium, a state of balance, before a disruption
questions.hint: It means a state of balance

questions.text: What is anchorage in media language?

options: The main image on a magazine cover
The speed at which a film is edited
Text, such as a caption, that fixes the meaning of an image
A small picture in the corner of a newspaper page

questions.solution: Anchorage (Barthes) is text that 'anchors' an image to one preferred meaning
questions.hint: Think about what an anchor does to a boat

questions.text: What term describes the way a text speaks to its audience, for example directly using 'you', or in a formal, distant way? Give the term.
questions.solution: Mode of address is how a text speaks to its audience, for example direct, informal, formal or friendly
questions.hint: Think about how a text 'speaks to' its reader

questions.text: On a magazine front cover, what is a cover line?

options: The name of the magazine at the top
The barcode and price
The photographer's name in tiny print
Text on the cover that tells readers about stories inside
feedback: That is the masthead

questions.solution: Cover lines advertise the stories and features inside the magazine
questions.hint: It 'sells' what is inside

questions.text: What is the term for a media text that mixes the conventions of two or more genres, such as a sci-fi western? Give the term.
questions.solution: A hybrid genre combines conventions of two or more genres
questions.hint: The same word is used for a car that runs on both petrol and electricity

questions.text: Which French theorist described five narrative codes, including the enigma code and the action code? Give the surname.
questions.solution: Roland Barthes described five codes, including the enigma (hermeneutic) code and the action (proairetic) code
questions.hint: He is also known for denotation, connotation and anchorage

questions.text: A perfume advert shows a red rose. The rose denotes a flower. What does it most likely connote?

options: A gardening tip
Romance and passion
The name of the perfume company
The time the advert was filmed

questions.solution: Red roses are conventionally associated with love, romance and passion
questions.hint: Think about when people give red roses

questions.text: A detective drama opens with an unanswered question: who sent the mysterious letter? Which of Barthes' codes is this?

options: Action code
Enigma code
Semantic code
Symbolic code
feedback: The action code is about actions that lead to further action
The semantic code is about the connotations of words and images
The symbolic code is about deeper meanings such as binary oppositions

questions.solution: The enigma (hermeneutic) code sets up a mystery or question that makes the audience want to find out more
questions.hint: Which code is about puzzles and questions?

questions.text: In a superhero film the hero is good, brave and selfless, while the villain is evil, cowardly and greedy. What term describes this pairing of opposites? Give the term.
questions.solution: Binary oppositions (Lévi-Strauss) are pairs of opposites, such as good and evil, that create conflict
questions.hint: Think of Lévi-Strauss

questions.text: A horror film poster uses a dark background, a dripping red font and a shadowy figure in a doorway. What are these examples of?

options: Audience demographics
Media regulation
Vertical integration
Genre codes and conventions

questions.solution: Dark colours, blood-red fonts and shadowy figures are codes and conventions of the horror genre
questions.hint: They tell you what kind of film it is

questions.text: In a fantasy story, a wise old woman gives the hero a magic sword, which he later uses to defeat the villain. Which of Propp's character types is the old woman? Give the term.

feedback.helper: The helper travels with the hero and aids them on the quest; giving a magical object is a different role
feedback.dispatcher: The dispatcher sends the hero on the quest

questions.solution: In Propp's theory the donor gives the hero a magical object or advice
questions.hint: She 'donates' something the hero needs

questions.text: A newspaper front page shows a photo of a crying child with the caption 'Forgotten by the council'. What does the caption do?

options: It denotes the time the photo was taken
It shows the paper's sales figures
It anchors the image, steering readers towards one meaning
It acts as the masthead

questions.solution: The caption anchors the image: it tells readers how to read the photo, here as a story of neglect
questions.hint: How would you read the photo without the caption?

questions.text: Read this film summary: 'A quiet village is attacked by a dragon. A young farmer realises what is happening, sets out to defeat it, and the village is rebuilt, stronger than before.' Which stage of Todorov's theory is 'the village is rebuilt'?

options: Disruption
Recognition of the disruption
Attempt to repair the disruption
New equilibrium
feedback: The disruption is the dragon's attack
The recognition is when the farmer realises what is happening
The attempt to repair is when the farmer sets out to defeat the dragon

questions.solution: Rebuilding the village, changed and stronger, is the new equilibrium at the end of the story
questions.hint: Match each sentence of the summary to a stage, in order

questions.text: Read this description of a magazine cover: 'The model looks straight at the camera, and the cover line says: You deserve this summer.' Which technique is used in both the image and the text?

options: Direct mode of address
Binary opposition
Restricted narration
Vertical integration

questions.solution: Eye contact and the word 'you' both speak directly to the reader: direct mode of address
questions.hint: Who are the model and the cover line speaking to?

questions.text: Read this: 'In the opening scene of a TV drama, a car speeds away and a door slams; the audience wonders what will happen next in the chase.' Which of Barthes' codes creates suspense through actions that lead to further action? Give the name of the code.

feedback.enigma code: The enigma code is a question or mystery; actions that lead to further action are a different code
feedback.enigma: The enigma code is a question or mystery; actions that lead to further action are a different code

questions.solution: Barthes' action (proairetic) code creates suspense through actions that make us expect what will happen next
questions.hint: The code is named after what happens physically

questions.text: A Western film poster shows a cowboy hat, a horse, a desert and a saloon. What is the term for familiar objects and settings like these that signal the genre?

options: Anchorage
Demographics
Synergy
Iconography

questions.solution: Iconography is the set of visual signs (props, costumes, settings) that signal a genre
questions.hint: The word contains 'icon', meaning an image

questions.text: Which pair of signs on a front cover would most clearly connote luxury?

options: Gold lettering and a model in an expensive evening dress
A cartoon dog and bright primary colours
Handwritten text and a messy bedroom
A muddy football boot and a torn shirt

questions.solution: Gold and expensive evening wear are conventionally associated with wealth and luxury
questions.hint: Work out what each pair connotes, then pick the one linked to wealth

questions.text: Explain how the front cover of a magazine uses media language to attract its target audience. Use two examples of codes or conventions.

rubric.model_answer: The masthead is large and bold in the magazine's house style, so regular readers recognise it instantly. The main image uses direct mode of address: the model makes eye contact with the reader, creating a personal connection. Cover lines using words such as 'you' and 'exclusive' promise content that suits the audience's interests.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: first code or convention identified
1 mark: how it attracts the target audience
1 mark: second code or convention identified
1 mark: how it attracts the target audience

questions.solution: Masthead, main image, mode of address, cover lines, colour and typography all attract the audience
questions.hint: Pick two features of the cover, then explain who each one appeals to and why

questions.text: Which statement about Todorov's narrative theory is accurate?

options: It says every story must have exactly eight character types
It argues that audiences decode texts in three different ways
It describes a pattern from equilibrium through disruption to a new equilibrium that differs from the start
It states that the new equilibrium is always identical to the first
feedback: Character types come from Propp
Three readings come from Stuart Hall
Todorov's new equilibrium is stable again but different from the start

questions.solution: Todorov's pattern ends in a new equilibrium: the situation is stable again but changed
questions.hint: Think about whether the ending is the same as the beginning

questions.text: Why might a producer use familiar genre conventions in a new TV crime drama?

options: It makes the drama exempt from regulation
It guarantees the drama will win awards
Audiences recognise them quickly, which sets up expectations and reduces financial risk
It means no script needs to be written

questions.solution: Familiar conventions attract audiences who know and like the genre, making success more likely
questions.hint: Think about what audiences expect and what producers want to avoid

questions.text: Which statement about Propp's theory is accurate?

options: It explains how audiences are directly affected by violent media
It describes the five stages of equilibrium and disruption
It is a theory of media ownership
It identifies character functions, such as hero, villain and donor, that recur across folk tales
feedback: That is the idea of the hypodermic needle (effects) model
That is Todorov's theory

questions.solution: Propp found that Russian folk tales reuse the same character functions, such as hero, villain and donor
questions.hint: Remember what Propp studied

questions.text: A critic says a superhero film reinforces the binary opposition of order versus chaos. What does this mean?

options: The film has two separate endings
The film was shot in two different countries
The film is aimed at two different age groups
The story is built on a conflict between two opposed ideas, order and chaos

questions.solution: A binary opposition is a pair of opposed ideas; the conflict between them drives the story
questions.hint: Think about what 'binary' means

questions.text: Why do magazine covers often show the model looking directly at the reader?

options: It is required by the press regulator
It hides the barcode
It makes the cover lines easier to print
Direct eye contact creates a personal relationship that draws the reader in

questions.solution: Direct address through eye contact makes the reader feel personally spoken to
questions.hint: Think about how it feels when someone looks straight at you

questions.text: Explain how binary oppositions can create conflict in a narrative. Refer to an example of your own.

rubric.model_answer: Lévi-Strauss argued that narratives are organised around pairs of opposites, such as good/evil or nature/technology. In a superhero film, the hero represents order and safety while the villain represents chaos. The clash between these opposites drives the conflict, and the resolution usually shows which value the text favours, revealing its ideology.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: binary oppositions explained as pairs of opposites (Lévi-Strauss)
1 mark: a relevant example of a binary opposition
1 mark: how the opposition creates conflict in the story
1 mark: how the resolution reveals the values or ideology of the text

questions.solution: Pairs of opposites drive conflict, and the ending shows which side the text favours
questions.hint: Start with a pair of opposites in a story you know

questions.text: In media studies, what is a stereotype?

options: An oversimplified, generalised image of a group of people
A completely accurate picture of every individual
A type of camera shot
A company that owns many media brands

questions.solution: A stereotype reduces a group of people to a few simple, generalised traits
questions.hint: Think about 'oversimplified'

questions.text: What term describes the way the media 'stand in the middle' between real events and the audience, shaping how events are presented? Give the term.
questions.solution: Mediation is the process by which producers select and shape reality before it reaches the audience
questions.hint: The word shares its root with 'media' and 'medium'

questions.text: Who introduced the idea of the 'male gaze' in film?

options: Stuart Hall
David Gauntlett
Laura Mulvey
Vladimir Propp
feedback: Stuart Hall is known for representation and reception theory
David Gauntlett is known for identity theory
Propp is known for character types in folk tales

questions.solution: Laura Mulvey introduced the male gaze in her 1975 essay on narrative cinema
questions.hint: She is a British feminist film theorist

questions.text: What term describes a representation that deliberately goes against a stereotype, such as a female engineer in a male-dominated field? Give the term.
questions.solution: A countertype challenges a stereotype by showing a group in an unexpected way
questions.hint: Its name suggests going against the usual 'type'

questions.text: In media studies, which phrase defines representation?

options: The number of people who watch a programme
The legal control of media content
The order of events in a story
The way the media re-present people, places, groups and ideas to an audience

questions.solution: Representation is how the media re-present the world: people, places, groups, events and ideas
questions.hint: Split the word: re-present

questions.text: What does 'misrepresentation' mean?

options: Showing a group often and fairly
Measuring the size of an audience
Giving a film an age certificate
Showing a person or group in an inaccurate or distorted way

questions.solution: Misrepresentation is showing a person or group inaccurately or in a distorted way
questions.hint: The prefix 'mis-' means wrongly

questions.text: Which theorist argued that the media give people 'tools' to build their own sense of identity? Give the surname.
questions.solution: David Gauntlett argues that audiences use media as resources, or tools, to construct their identities
questions.hint: He is a British theorist who writes about identity and creativity

questions.text: What is the difference between selection and construction in representation?

options: Selection is how material is put together; construction is choosing what to leave out
Selection is choosing what to include or leave out; construction is how the material is put together
Selection is about the audience; construction is about regulation
There is no difference: both are words for a stereotype
feedback: You have swapped them round

questions.solution: Producers select what to include, then construct it into a text through editing, framing and layout
questions.hint: One happens before the other

questions.text: In Stuart Hall's view, how does stereotyping work?

options: It happens only in advertising aimed at children
It reduces people to a few simple traits, and tends to occur where there are inequalities of power
It always gives a fair and complete picture of a group
It is caused only by audiences, never by producers

questions.solution: Hall argued that stereotyping reduces people to a few simple characteristics and is linked to inequalities of power
questions.hint: Think about who usually has the power to represent others

questions.text: What is the term for including just one person from an under-represented group in a cast, mainly to appear diverse? Give the term.
questions.solution: Tokenism is a small, symbolic effort to include a group without real representation
questions.hint: It comes from the phrase for a small symbolic gesture

questions.text: What did Laura Mulvey mean by the 'male gaze'?

options: Films often position the audience to look at women as objects, from a male point of view
Men watch more films than women do
Male directors use more close-ups than female directors
Male characters always look directly at the camera

questions.solution: Mulvey argued mainstream cinema often frames women as objects to be looked at, from a male point of view
questions.hint: Think about whose point of view the camera takes

questions.text: What is the name of the test which asks whether a film has at least two named women who talk to each other about something other than a man? Give the name.
questions.solution: The Bechdel test is a simple check of how women are represented in films
questions.hint: It is named after an American cartoonist

questions.text: What is self-representation?

options: When people create and share their own image, for example on social media
When the media show a group only through stereotypes
When a regulator decides how groups are shown
When a news story is told from the police's point of view

questions.solution: Self-representation is people presenting themselves, for example through social media posts and profiles
questions.hint: Who is doing the representing?

questions.text: What term describes the way news producers choose a particular angle and emphasis that shapes how a story is understood? Give the term.

feedback.agenda setting: Agenda setting is about which stories get covered; the angle and emphasis of one story is something else

questions.solution: Framing is presenting a story from a particular angle, which shapes how audiences understand it
questions.hint: Think of what the border of a picture does to what you see

questions.text: A TV advert for cleaning products shows only women doing housework while men relax. What is this an example of?

options: A countertype
Self-representation
A gender stereotype
Vertical integration
feedback: A countertype would go against the stereotype
Self-representation is when people represent themselves

questions.solution: Showing only women doing housework repeats a traditional gender stereotype
questions.hint: Is this an expected or an unexpected image of women?

questions.text: A news report about a protest shows only images of a small group damaging property, not the thousands marching peacefully. Which process of representation does this show most clearly?

options: Hybridity
Synergy
Selection
Convergence

questions.solution: The editors selected some images and left others out, shaping how the protest is represented
questions.hint: Think about what was chosen and what was left out

questions.text: A study finds that older people appear in very few of a TV channel's programmes compared with how many older people there are in the population. What term describes this? Give the term.
questions.solution: Under-representation means a group appears in the media far less than it does in real life
questions.hint: The group appears less than it should

questions.text: A music video shows a female rapper as powerful and in control of her career. How does this relate to stereotypes?

options: It is an example of the male gaze
It is an example of vertical integration
It reinforces the stereotype that women are passive
It challenges stereotypes of women as passive

questions.solution: Showing a woman as powerful and in control challenges the stereotype of women as passive
questions.hint: Compare the image with the traditional stereotype

questions.text: A series of films always shows scientists as older men in white lab coats with wild hair. What are these repeated, oversimplified images of scientists an example of? Give the term.

feedback.archetype: An archetype is a universal original model of a character; repeated, oversimplified images of a group have another name

questions.solution: Repeated, oversimplified images of a group are stereotypes
questions.hint: The word was first used in printing, for a plate that made identical copies

questions.text: An advert shows an elderly woman skateboarding confidently. How does this representation relate to stereotypes of older people?

options: It reinforces them by presenting older people as frail
It is an example of the male gaze
It challenges them by presenting older people as active and capable
It is an example of media regulation

questions.solution: Showing an older person as active and confident goes against the stereotype of older people as frail
questions.hint: Compare the advert with the usual stereotype of older people

questions.text: Read this headline and photo description: 'TEEN THUGS RUN RIOT', above a photo of three hooded teenagers in a dark street. How are young people represented?

options: Positively, as active members of the community
Neutrally, with no connotations
Negatively, as threatening and lawless, reinforcing a stereotype
As a countertype to the usual image of teenagers

questions.solution: The words 'thugs' and 'riot', hoods and darkness all connote threat, reinforcing a negative stereotype of youth
questions.hint: Look at the connotations of the words and the image separately, then together

questions.text: Read this: 'In a sample of 50 adverts, 40 showed women at home and 10 showed women at work.' What percentage showed women at work, and what does this suggest?

options: 80%, suggesting women were mostly represented in work roles
10%, suggesting women were never shown at work
20%, suggesting women were mostly represented in domestic roles
25%, suggesting an equal balance of roles
feedback: 80% is the share showing women at home
10 is the number of adverts, not the percentage
10 out of 40 would be 25%, but the total is 50 adverts

questions.solution: 10 out of 50 is 20%, so 80% showed women at home: a mainly domestic representation
questions.hint: First work out 10 out of 50 as a percentage

questions.text: Read this: 'A documentary editor removes every interview that disagrees with the film's argument.' Which process of representation is the editor using? Give the term.

feedback.construction: Construction is how the chosen material is put together; deciding what to leave out comes first

questions.solution: The editor is selecting what to include and leaving out other views, which shapes the representation
questions.hint: Think about what is being kept and what is being cut

questions.text: A magazine digitally edits a model's photo to remove every skin blemish and wrinkle. Which concern about representation does this raise?

options: It makes the magazine illegal to sell
It constructs an unrealistic image that audiences may come to see as normal
It is an example of vertical integration
It proves the magazine is aimed at men

questions.solution: Digital editing constructs an idealised image; repeated exposure can make unrealistic standards seem normal
questions.hint: Is the edited photo a realistic image of a person?

questions.text: Read this description: 'A news bulletin about a city lists crime figures, and every image shows run-down streets; no parks, schools or businesses are shown.' What effect is this representation of the city most likely to have?

options: It gives a complete and balanced picture of the city
It presents the city as threatening and deprived, leaving out other aspects
It challenges negative stereotypes of the city
It is an example of self-representation

questions.solution: By selecting only crime and run-down streets, the bulletin constructs a narrow, negative image of the city
questions.hint: Notice what was shown and what was left out

questions.text: Explain how a media text could challenge a stereotype of a social group. Use an example of your own.

rubric.model_answer: A TV drama could show a teenage character as responsible and caring, for example looking after a younger sibling and doing well at school, rather than as lazy or antisocial. By giving the character depth, positive actions and a central role, the text offers a countertype that encourages the audience to question the usual negative image of teenagers.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: a relevant stereotype identified
1 mark: how the text presents the group differently (a countertype)
1 mark: the media language used to do this (e.g. role, narrative, camera, dialogue)
1 mark: the possible effect on the audience's view of the group

questions.solution: A countertype gives the group depth and positive, unexpected qualities
questions.hint: Start by naming the stereotype, then describe how a text could show the opposite

questions.text: Which statement about representation is accurate?

options: Documentaries show reality exactly as it is, with no choices made
Only fictional texts contain representations
Representations never affect how audiences see real groups
All media representations are constructed, so they always involve choices by producers
feedback: Documentary makers still choose what to film, include and leave out
News and documentaries contain representations too

questions.solution: Every representation, even in news and documentary, is constructed through selection and choices
questions.hint: Think about whether any text can show reality with no choices at all

questions.text: Why might advertisers rely on stereotypes?

options: They are required by the Advertising Standards Authority
They always show groups accurately
They communicate quickly and clearly in a short time, using ideas the audience already recognises
They make adverts longer and more detailed

questions.solution: Adverts are short, so stereotypes are a quick shorthand that audiences recognise instantly
questions.hint: Think about how long an advert lasts

questions.text: Which statement about Tessa Perkins' view of stereotypes is accurate?

options: She argued that stereotypes are always false and only about minority groups
She argued that stereotypes are not always negative or completely false, and can change over time
She introduced the idea of the male gaze
She argued that audiences are always passive
feedback: The male gaze comes from Laura Mulvey

questions.solution: Perkins (1979) argued that stereotypes are not always negative, not always about minorities and not always false
questions.hint: Perkins questioned common assumptions about stereotypes

questions.text: Why can social media change how groups are represented?

options: Social media posts are not mediated in any way
Members of groups can create self-representations instead of relying on traditional media producers
Social media are banned from showing people
Social media only show celebrities
feedback: People still select, edit and filter what they post, so it is still mediated

questions.solution: Social media lets people represent themselves, though their posts are still selected and constructed
questions.hint: Think about who is creating the content

questions.text: A news channel always chooses a middle-aged white man to comment on the economy. What is the most accurate criticism?

options: It breaks the 9pm watershed rule
It is an example of a countertype
It shows the channel uses vertical integration
It may suggest that only one kind of person has expertise, under-representing others

questions.solution: Always choosing the same kind of expert under-represents other groups and suggests only they have expertise
questions.hint: Think about who is missing

questions.text: Explain how mediation affects the representation of real events in the news.

rubric.model_answer: News is never a direct window on reality. Journalists and editors select which events count as news and which images and interviews to use or leave out. They then construct the story through headlines, framing, camera angles and editing. Each choice reflects news values and the outlet's viewpoint, so audiences receive a shaped version of the event that can make some groups or views seem more important than others.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: mediation explained as the media shaping reality between event and audience
1 mark: selection explained (what is included or left out)
1 mark: construction explained (e.g. headlines, framing, editing)
1 mark: the effect on the audience's understanding
1 mark: link to the values or viewpoint of the producer

questions.solution: Selection and construction shape news, so audiences get a version of events, not reality itself
questions.hint: Follow a story from the real event, through the newsroom, to the audience

questions.text: What is a media conglomerate?

options: A small independent production company
A large company that owns many different media businesses
A government body that regulates the press
A type of camera shot

questions.solution: A conglomerate is a large corporation that owns many companies across different media
questions.hint: The word suggests things gathered together

questions.text: Which UK organisation gives age certificates such as U, PG, 12A, 15 and 18 to films? Give the name or abbreviation.

feedback.Ofcom: Ofcom regulates TV, radio and on-demand services, not film certificates

questions.solution: The BBFC (British Board of Film Classification) classifies films and videos in the UK
questions.hint: Its full name begins 'British Board of'

questions.text: Which UK organisation regulates the content of adverts in all media?

options: British Board of Film Classification (BBFC)
Pan European Game Information (PEGI)
Advertising Standards Authority (ASA)
Broadcasters' Audience Research Board (BARB)

questions.solution: The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) regulates advertising across UK media
questions.hint: Look for the word 'advertising' in the name

questions.text: Which system gives age ratings such as 3, 7, 12, 16 and 18 to video games in the UK and Europe?

options: PEGI
BBFC
Ofcom
IPSO
feedback: The BBFC classifies films and videos
Ofcom regulates broadcasting
IPSO regulates newspapers and magazines

questions.solution: PEGI (Pan European Game Information) gives age ratings to video games
questions.hint: Its name refers to games across Europe

questions.text: John Reith, who set out the aim to 'inform, educate and entertain', was the first Director-General of which UK broadcaster? Give the name.
questions.solution: John Reith was the first Director-General of the BBC, and his aim shaped public service broadcasting
questions.hint: It began radio broadcasts in 1922

questions.text: What is convergence in the media?

options: A government ban on certain programmes
The coming together of different media technologies and industries, such as phones that stream TV
The process of giving a film an age rating
The way a story moves from disruption to equilibrium

questions.solution: Convergence is the merging of media technologies and industries, for example one device for TV, music and news
questions.hint: Think of one device that does many media jobs

questions.text: What term describes one company owning businesses at different stages of the same process, such as making, distributing and showing films? Give the term.

feedback.horizontal integration: Horizontal integration means owning several companies at the same stage, such as rival studios
feedback.horizontal: Horizontal integration means owning several companies at the same stage, such as rival studios

questions.solution: Vertical integration means owning several stages of the chain, such as production, distribution and exhibition
questions.hint: Picture the stages as a ladder from making to showing

questions.text: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal integration?

options: Vertical: owning several firms at the same stage; horizontal: owning different stages of one process
Vertical: owning different stages of one process; horizontal: owning several firms at the same stage
Vertical: working in one country; horizontal: working worldwide
Vertical: print media; horizontal: online media
feedback: You have swapped them round

questions.solution: Vertical integration covers different stages of a process; horizontal integration covers firms at the same stage
questions.hint: Think of a ladder (stages) and a row (rivals side by side)

questions.text: What does the 9pm watershed on UK television mean?

options: All programmes must end by 9pm
Material unsuitable for children should not normally be shown before 9pm
Adverts are banned after 9pm
Children's channels must close at 9pm

questions.solution: The watershed means content unsuitable for children should generally not be shown before 9pm
questions.hint: It is a rule designed to protect children

questions.text: What is the term for a strategy in which different parts of one company work together to promote a product, such as a film, its soundtrack and its toys? Give the term.
questions.solution: Synergy is cross-promotion across a company's different products and platforms
questions.hint: The word comes from Greek for 'working together'

questions.text: Which independent organisation regulates most UK newspapers and magazines that choose to join it?

options: IPSO (Independent Press Standards Organisation)
BBFC (British Board of Film Classification)
PEGI (Pan European Game Information)
BARB (Broadcasters' Audience Research Board)

questions.solution: IPSO regulates the majority of UK newspapers and magazines through its Editors' Code
questions.hint: Look for the word 'press' in the name

questions.text: What term describes broadcasting that aims to serve the whole public by informing, educating and entertaining, rather than mainly making a profit? Give the term.

feedback.commercial broadcasting: Commercial broadcasting is mainly run to make a profit

questions.solution: Public service broadcasting (PSB) aims to serve all audiences and the public interest
questions.hint: Its abbreviation is three letters, starting with P

questions.text: Which of these is an example of self-regulation?

options: A government passing a law banning a magazine
A court sending a journalist to prison
Newspapers agreeing to follow a code of practice run by an industry body
A viewer switching off a programme

questions.solution: Self-regulation means an industry sets and enforces its own rules, as the press does through IPSO
questions.hint: Who makes and enforces the rules in self-regulation?

questions.text: Which regulator deals with complaints about UK TV and radio programmes and was set up in 2003? Give the name.

feedback.BBFC: The BBFC classifies films and videos

questions.solution: Ofcom regulates UK broadcasting, as well as phone and postal services
questions.hint: It also regulates phone and postal services

questions.text: A film studio also owns a chain of cinemas where its films are shown. What is this an example of?

options: Horizontal integration
Self-representation
Vertical integration
Hybridity
feedback: Horizontal integration means owning several businesses at the same stage

questions.solution: Owning both production and exhibition is vertical integration
questions.hint: Are the businesses at the same stage or at different stages?

questions.text: A video game includes realistic violence and strong language. Which system would give it an age rating in the UK?

options: BBFC
Ofcom
PEGI
IPSO

questions.solution: Video games in the UK are given PEGI age ratings
questions.hint: Which system is designed for games?

questions.text: A newspaper owner buys two rival newspapers. Which type of integration is this? Give the term.

feedback.vertical integration: Vertical integration is owning different stages of a process; buying rivals at the same stage is different
feedback.vertical: Vertical integration is owning different stages of a process; buying rivals at the same stage is different

questions.solution: Buying rivals at the same stage of the industry is horizontal integration
questions.hint: The businesses are side by side at the same stage

questions.text: A streaming service charges a monthly payment for access to its films and series. Which funding model is this?

options: Licence fee
Subscription
Advertising only
Public donations

questions.solution: A regular payment for access is a subscription model
questions.hint: Think about what you pay every month

questions.text: A smartphone lets its user watch TV, read a newspaper and listen to the radio on one device. Which industry trend does this show? Give the term.
questions.solution: Convergence is the coming together of different media on one device or platform
questions.hint: Several media have come together in one place

questions.text: A TV channel shows a programme with strong violence at 7pm, and viewers complain. Which organisation would investigate?

options: BBFC
PEGI
ASA
Ofcom
feedback: The BBFC classifies films and videos, not TV broadcasts
PEGI rates video games
The ASA regulates adverts, not programmes

questions.solution: Ofcom regulates TV and enforces rules such as the 9pm watershed
questions.hint: Which regulator covers TV programmes?

questions.text: Read this: 'Company X owns a film studio, a film distribution company and a cinema chain. It also owns two other film studios.' Which types of integration does Company X show?

options: Vertical integration only
Horizontal integration only
Neither type of integration
Vertical and horizontal integration

questions.solution: Studio, distributor and cinemas are different stages (vertical); three studios are at the same stage (horizontal)
questions.hint: Check the different stages first, then check for several firms at one stage

questions.text: Read this: 'A small independent games studio launches its game online, using social media and fan communities instead of expensive TV adverts.' Why might the studio choose this marketing method?

options: It is required by PEGI
It reaches a large audience cheaply, which suits a smaller budget
TV adverts for games are illegal in the UK
Social media marketing guarantees higher sales than any other method

questions.solution: Online and fan-based marketing is low-cost and can reach many people, ideal for a small budget
questions.hint: Think about the studio's budget

questions.text: Read this: 'A 2011 scandal about journalists hacking phones led to a public inquiry into the culture and ethics of the British press.' What was this inquiry called? Give the name.
questions.solution: The Leveson Inquiry (2011–2012) examined the culture, practices and ethics of the British press
questions.hint: It was named after the judge who led it

questions.text: Read this: 'Channel 4 is publicly owned but is funded mainly by advertising.' Which statement follows from this?

options: Channel 4 is a public service broadcaster with a commercial funding model
Channel 4 is funded by the licence fee
Channel 4 is owned by a private conglomerate
Channel 4 is not regulated by Ofcom

questions.solution: Public ownership with advertising income means a public service broadcaster funded commercially
questions.hint: Use both facts in the statement: who owns it, and how it is funded

questions.text: A media company buys a rival so that it controls most of its market. Why might regulators be concerned?

options: It makes the company's products cheaper to regulate
It automatically breaks the 9pm watershed
Less competition may mean less choice and fewer viewpoints for audiences
It means the company must close its websites

questions.solution: Concentrated ownership reduces competition, which can limit choice and the range of viewpoints
questions.hint: Think about what happens to competition

questions.text: Explain why media regulation is needed. Give two reasons.

rubric.model_answer: Regulation protects children from unsuitable content, for example through BBFC age ratings and the 9pm watershed. It also protects the public from inaccurate or unfair content, such as misleading adverts (ASA) or press intrusion into privacy (IPSO), so that audiences can trust what they see and people's rights are respected.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: first reason (e.g. protecting children)
1 mark: developed with an example of a regulator or rule
1 mark: second reason (e.g. accuracy, fairness, privacy, honest advertising)
1 mark: developed with an example of a regulator or rule

questions.solution: Regulation protects children and protects the public from misleading, unfair or intrusive content
questions.hint: Think about who regulation protects and from what

questions.text: Which statement about public service broadcasting in the UK is accurate?

options: It aims to serve the public interest, with duties such as news and programmes for different audiences
It is broadcasting that is free from all regulation
It only shows programmes that make a profit
It is only available through paid subscription services

questions.solution: Public service broadcasters have duties to serve the public, such as impartial news and varied programming
questions.hint: Think about the aim to inform, educate and entertain

questions.text: Why do large conglomerates often have an advantage over small independent media companies?

options: They are exempt from regulation by Ofcom
They are not allowed to advertise
They can spread financial risk across many products and use synergy to promote them
They never need to attract an audience

questions.solution: Conglomerates can absorb losses on some products and cross-promote across their many platforms
questions.hint: Think about money and promotion

questions.text: Which statement about the BBFC is accurate?

options: It regulates newspapers and magazines
It gives age ratings to video games across Europe
It classifies films and videos in the UK, giving age ratings and content advice
It is the BBC's own film studio
feedback: That is IPSO
That is PEGI
The BBFC is an independent body, not part of the BBC

questions.solution: The BBFC classifies films and videos with age ratings and short content advice
questions.hint: Remember what the letters BBFC stand for

questions.text: Why might a newspaper put its website content behind a paywall?

options: To earn money from readers as print sales and advertising income fall
Because IPSO requires all newspapers to charge online
To stop the paper from being regulated
Because paywalls increase the number of free readers

questions.solution: Paywalls bring in subscription money to replace falling print sales and advertising income
questions.hint: Think about where newspapers get their money

questions.text: Which statement best explains how convergence has changed the media industry?

options: Convergence means each company may only use one platform
Audiences access content across many devices, so companies produce for many platforms at once
Convergence has stopped people using smartphones for media
Convergence means films can no longer be shown in cinemas

questions.solution: Because audiences use many devices, companies now make and distribute content across platforms
questions.hint: Think about how you access media on different devices

questions.text: Explain how media ownership can affect the content that audiences receive.

rubric.model_answer: When a few large conglomerates own many outlets, they can shape what is produced. Owners may favour content that makes the most profit, such as sequels and franchises, so riskier or niche content gets less funding. Concentrated ownership may also reduce the range of viewpoints, as outlets with the same owner may share similar values. Synergy lets one company cross-promote its own products across its platforms.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: concentration of ownership explained
1 mark: the profit motive leads to safe or mainstream content
1 mark: a reduced range of viewpoints or diversity
1 mark: synergy or cross-promotion of the owner's products
1 mark: a clear link to what audiences receive

questions.solution: Ownership affects content through profit motives, the range of viewpoints and synergy
questions.hint: Think about what owners want and how that shapes what gets made

questions.text: What is a target audience?

options: The specific group of people a media text is aimed at
Everyone who lives in the UK
The people who make a media text
The regulator that checks a text

questions.solution: A target audience is the particular group a text is designed to appeal to
questions.hint: Think of a 'target' that is aimed at

questions.text: Which term describes classifying an audience by facts such as age, gender, income and occupation? Give the term.

feedback.psychographics: Psychographics groups people by values, attitudes and lifestyles
feedback.psychographic: Psychographics groups people by values, attitudes and lifestyles

questions.solution: Demographics group audiences by measurable facts such as age, gender, income and occupation
questions.hint: The word begins with a Greek root meaning 'people'

questions.text: Which model suggests that the media 'inject' messages directly into a passive audience?

options: Uses and gratifications theory
The two-step flow model
The hypodermic needle model
Reception theory
feedback: Uses and gratifications sees the audience as active
The two-step flow model says messages pass through opinion leaders
Reception theory says audiences decode texts in different ways

questions.solution: The hypodermic needle model sees the audience as passive, with messages 'injected' directly
questions.hint: Think of an injection

questions.text: Which term describes classifying an audience by their values, attitudes, interests and lifestyles? Give the term.

feedback.demographics: Demographics groups people by facts such as age, gender and income
feedback.demographic: Demographics groups people by facts such as age, gender and income

questions.solution: Psychographics groups audiences by values, attitudes and lifestyles rather than facts like age
questions.hint: The word begins with a root linked to the mind

questions.text: Who developed the uses and gratifications theory?

options: Blumler and Katz
Lazarsfeld and Mulvey
Gerbner and Todorov
Propp and Hall

questions.solution: Jay Blumler and Elihu Katz developed uses and gratifications theory in the 1970s
questions.hint: The theorists' surnames begin with B and K

questions.text: Which theorist is linked with cultivation theory?

options: George Gerbner
Stuart Hall
Vladimir Propp
Laura Mulvey
feedback: Stuart Hall is linked with reception theory
Propp is linked with character types in folk tales
Laura Mulvey is linked with the male gaze

questions.solution: George Gerbner developed cultivation theory about the long-term effects of heavy TV viewing
questions.hint: He studied the long-term effects of television

questions.text: In the two-step flow model, what name is given to the people who receive media messages first and then pass them on to others, with their own interpretation? Give the term.
questions.solution: In the two-step flow model, opinion leaders interpret media messages and pass them on to others
questions.hint: They are respected people whose views others follow

questions.text: What is the difference between a mass audience and a niche audience?

options: A mass audience is small and specialised; a niche audience is large and varied
A mass audience is large and varied; a niche audience is a small, specialised group
A mass audience only reads print; a niche audience only uses social media
A mass audience is always older; a niche audience is always younger
feedback: You have swapped them round

questions.solution: Mass audiences are large and varied; niche audiences are small groups with specific interests
questions.hint: Think of a mass of people and a small niche

questions.text: In uses and gratifications theory, what is the 'diversion' (entertainment) need?

options: Using media to find out what is happening in the world
Using media to escape everyday problems and relax
Using media to compare oneself with characters
Using media to have something to talk about with friends
feedback: That is the information (surveillance) need
That is the personal identity need
That is the social interaction (personal relationships) need

questions.solution: Diversion is using media for escapism, entertainment and relaxation
questions.hint: To 'divert' is to turn away from something

questions.text: In Stuart Hall's reception theory, what is the name for the reading that accepts the meaning the producer intended? Give the term.

feedback.negotiated reading: A negotiated reading accepts some of the message but not all of it
feedback.oppositional reading: An oppositional reading rejects the intended meaning

questions.solution: The preferred (dominant) reading accepts the meaning the producer encoded
questions.hint: It is the meaning the producer wanted the audience to take

questions.text: What is an active audience?

options: An audience that does physical exercise while watching
An audience that accepts every message without thinking
An audience that interprets, questions and chooses the media texts it uses
An audience that only watches live television
feedback: That describes a passive audience

questions.solution: An active audience makes choices and interprets texts rather than simply absorbing them
questions.hint: The opposite of a passive audience

questions.text: What is the term for a person who both consumes and produces media content, such as a vlogger who also watches other people's videos? Give the term.
questions.solution: A prosumer both produces and consumes media
questions.hint: The word blends 'producer' and 'consumer'

questions.text: What is the difference between a primary and a secondary audience?

options: A primary audience is the main group a text is aimed at; a secondary audience is another group that also uses it
A primary audience is the youngest viewers; a secondary audience is the oldest
A primary audience watches live; a secondary audience records programmes
A primary audience pays for the text; a secondary audience is the regulator

questions.solution: The primary audience is the main target; a secondary audience is another group that also consumes the text
questions.hint: Think about who the text is mainly aimed at

questions.text: Which UK organisation measures television audience figures? Give the name or abbreviation.

feedback.Ofcom: Ofcom regulates broadcasting; it does not produce the audience figures

questions.solution: BARB (Broadcasters' Audience Research Board) measures UK TV audiences
questions.hint: Its four-letter abbreviation starts with B

questions.text: A viewer watches a cookery programme to learn new recipes. Which need from uses and gratifications theory is being met?

options: Diversion
Personal identity
Social interaction
Information (surveillance)

questions.solution: Learning something useful from the media meets the information (surveillance) need
questions.hint: Is the viewer escaping, learning, comparing themselves, or socialising?

questions.text: A viewer watches a reality TV show so she has something to discuss with her friends at school the next day. Which need is being met?

options: Diversion
Information (surveillance)
Social interaction (personal relationships)
Personal identity

questions.solution: Using media to have something to share with others meets the social interaction need
questions.hint: Think about why her friends matter here

questions.text: A gamer reads a review that criticises a game's violence. He agrees the game is too violent for young children, but still thinks it is mostly harmless fun. In Hall's reception theory, what kind of reading is this? Give the term.

feedback.oppositional reading: An oppositional reading rejects the message completely; he agrees with part of it
feedback.preferred reading: A preferred reading accepts the whole message; he only agrees with part of it

questions.solution: A negotiated reading accepts part of the message and rejects part of it
questions.hint: He accepts some of the review's message but not all of it

questions.text: A teenager who watches many crime dramas starts to believe that her quiet town is much more dangerous than it really is. Which theory explains this?

options: Cultivation theory
Uses and gratifications
Two-step flow
Reception theory

questions.solution: Cultivation theory suggests heavy viewing gradually shapes beliefs about reality, the 'mean world' effect
questions.hint: The belief has grown slowly through heavy viewing

questions.text: A viewer watches a political advert and completely rejects its message, deciding the opposite is true. In Hall's reception theory, what kind of reading is this? Give the term.

feedback.negotiated reading: A negotiated reading accepts part of the message; this viewer rejects all of it

questions.solution: An oppositional reading rejects the producer's intended meaning
questions.hint: The viewer completely disagrees with the intended message

questions.text: A magazine describes its readers as '18–30, urban, interested in sustainable fashion and ethical living'. Which part of this description is psychographic?

options: Aged 18–30
Interested in sustainable fashion and ethical living
Living in urban areas
Being readers of a magazine

questions.solution: Interests and values are psychographic; age and location are demographic
questions.hint: Psychographics is about values and interests, not facts like age

questions.text: Read these audience figures for a TV series: 'Episode 1: 4.2 million viewers. Episode 6: 2.1 million viewers.' What is the percentage change from episode 1 to episode 6?

options: A fall of 50%
A rise of 50%
A fall of 21%
A fall of 2.1%

questions.solution: The audience fell by 2.1 million from 4.2 million: 2.1 ÷ 4.2 = 0.5, a fall of 50%
questions.hint: Work out the change, then divide by the original figure

questions.text: Read this: 'Researchers in the 1940s found that most voters were influenced more by people they knew than directly by newspapers and radio.' Which model was developed from findings like these?

options: The hypodermic needle model
Cultivation theory
The male gaze
The two-step flow model
feedback: The hypodermic needle model says media affect people directly
Cultivation theory is about the long-term effects of heavy TV viewing

questions.solution: Lazarsfeld and Katz's two-step flow model says media influence often passes through opinion leaders
questions.hint: The influence came through other people, not directly

questions.text: Read this: 'In 1938, a radio drama about an alien invasion was reported to have caused panic among some listeners.' Critics have used this example to support which model of media effects? Give the name.
questions.solution: The reported panic was used to support the hypodermic needle (magic bullet) model of direct effects
questions.hint: The model compares media messages to an injection

questions.text: Read this: 'Heavy viewers of TV news are more likely than light viewers to say the world is a frightening place.' Which theory does this finding support?

options: Uses and gratifications theory
The two-step flow model
Propp's character theory
Cultivation theory

questions.solution: Cultivation theory predicts that heavy viewers come to see the world as more threatening ('mean world syndrome')
questions.hint: Compare heavy and light viewers

questions.text: Read this audience profile: 'Mainly social grades A and B; aged 35–55; reads long articles on politics and business.' Which product is most likely aimed at this audience?

options: A celebrity gossip magazine for teenagers
A children's comic
A gaming channel for under-12s
A quality newspaper with in-depth news

questions.solution: Grades A and B are professional and managerial; older readers interested in politics and business suit a quality newspaper
questions.hint: Use the age, the social grades and the interests together

questions.text: Explain how uses and gratifications theory sees audiences differently from the hypodermic needle model.

rubric.model_answer: The hypodermic needle model sees the audience as passive: media messages are 'injected' and directly change behaviour, affecting everyone in the same way. Uses and gratifications (Blumler and Katz) sees the audience as active: people choose media to meet their own needs, such as information, personal identity, social interaction and diversion, so different people use the same text in different ways.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: hypodermic needle model sees a passive audience
1 mark: direct, uniform effects explained
1 mark: uses and gratifications sees an active audience choosing media
1 mark: at least one named need (information, identity, social interaction, diversion)

questions.solution: One model has a passive audience receiving direct effects; the other an active audience meeting its own needs
questions.hint: Start with whether each model sees the audience as active or passive

questions.text: What is the main criticism of the hypodermic needle model?

options: It suggests audiences are too active
It only applies to video games
It ignores that audiences are active and interpret messages in different ways
It was developed by Ofcom

questions.solution: Critics argue the model wrongly treats audiences as passive and identical
questions.hint: Think about how the model sees the audience

questions.text: Which statement about cultivation theory is accurate?

options: It argues that one advert can instantly change behaviour
It argues that audiences always reject media messages
It argues that heavy, long-term viewing can gradually shape people's view of reality
It is mainly about how stories are structured
feedback: Instant, direct effects are the idea of the hypodermic needle model
Story structure is narrative theory, such as Todorov's

questions.solution: Cultivation theory is about slow, cumulative effects of heavy viewing on beliefs about the world
questions.hint: Think about the word 'cultivate', as in growing something slowly

questions.text: Why do media producers research the demographics and psychographics of their audience?

options: Because Ofcom requires every company to publish them
To decide which regulator they belong to
To shape content and advertising that appeal to the people they want to reach
To guarantee that every viewer enjoys the text

questions.solution: Knowing who the audience is lets producers tailor content, marketing and advertising to them
questions.hint: Think about how producers make texts that sell

questions.text: Which statement about Hall's reception theory is accurate?

options: It suggests the same text can be decoded in different ways, depending on the audience
It says audiences always take the preferred reading
It explains how films are given age ratings
It describes the five stages of a narrative

questions.solution: Hall's encoding/decoding model says audiences may take a preferred, negotiated or oppositional reading
questions.hint: Remember the three kinds of reading

questions.text: Why has social media made audiences more active?

options: Social media users cannot choose what they see
Social media removes all advertising
Users can comment on, share, remix and create content, not only consume it
Social media audiences are always passive

questions.solution: Social media lets audiences respond to, share and create content, so they participate rather than just watch
questions.hint: Think about what users can do on social media besides watching

questions.text: Explain how cultivation theory could be used to argue that heavy TV viewing affects how people see the world.

rubric.model_answer: Gerbner's cultivation theory argues that repeated, long-term exposure to television gradually shapes viewers' beliefs. Because TV often shows crime and conflict, heavy viewers may come to believe the real world is more threatening than it is ('mean world syndrome'). The effect builds up slowly rather than instantly, and is strongest for heavy viewers who rely on TV for their picture of reality.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: Gerbner named or the theory summarised
1 mark: long-term, repeated exposure
1 mark: an example of the effect (e.g. mean world syndrome)
1 mark: the effect is cumulative and strongest for heavy viewers

questions.solution: Long-term heavy viewing slowly shapes beliefs, for example seeing the world as more threatening
questions.hint: Think about time: one programme, or years of viewing?
